title: Tariff Evasion Costs US Billions: White House Blames Transshipment
summary:
In a report released Thursday, August 13, 2026, the Trump White House alleged that countries are evading US tariffs by routing exports through third countries, a practice known as transshipping. The report estimates annual tax revenue losses of $19 billion to $26 billion.

The report specifically highlights China's response to 2018 tariffs: sending goods to nations like Mexico and Malaysia for packaging and limited assembly. This made it appear that US imports from China had dropped, while Beijing continued to expand its manufacturing sector. Peter Navarro, the White House trade adviser, told reporters that China is "laundering its exports" through more than 40 countries. "For years, the great transshipment scam has let communist China launder its exports," Navarro said.

The report arrives ahead of a planned September visit by Chinese Leader Xi Jinping, whom President Trump has described in flattering terms. Yet the Chinese government's export policies have destabilized auto, metals, and electronics sectors in the US, Europe, and Japan, according to the report. Navarro warned that India and others could also transship, and said new trade frameworks will penalize partners who engage in the practice.

To combat evasion, US Customs and Border Protection has begun using artificial intelligence in a prototype program to detect false origin claims. Importers caught falsifying origins can face retroactive tariffs going back about a year. The administration's tariffs have faced legal challenges, with the Supreme Court overturning some in February. While the US trade deficit remains large, it has narrowed by about $189 billion compared to the same period last year.
why_it_matters: When countries dodge import taxes, the effects ripple into prices, factory jobs, and how much governments can spend. If new trade frameworks penalize transshipment, the cost of everyday goods and the stability of global supply chains may shift while you are joining the workforce.

background_read: Tariffs are taxes a government charges on goods from another country; in 2018 the United States imposed broad tariffs on Chinese imports, beginning a trade conflict that reshaped global supply chains.

Xi Jinping has led China since 2013 as general secretary of the Communist Party and president; his government has tried to keep its export-heavy manufacturing sector growing even as the US and Europe challenge its industrial policies.

Peter Navarro is a long-time trade adviser who has pushed for aggressive tariffs on China; his transshipment argument is that goods are sent through places like Mexico and Malaysia for light finishing, so their final label hides their true origin.

US Customs and Border Protection is the federal agency that checks goods at borders and can penalize false origin claims; the Supreme Court, the highest US court, has also weighed in by striking down some of the administration's tariff rules.

Economists call this rerouting 'trade deflection': when direct flows fall, imports often rise from intermediate countries rather than disappearing, making it hard to tell how much policy really changes.

perspectives.description: The White House frames the report as a step toward protecting US manufacturing and tax revenue from cheating. Using artificial intelligence to detect false origin claims could make enforcement faster and more accurate, and the reported narrowing of the trade deficit may look like a sign of progress.

The report's own estimates describe billions in lost revenue, and the administration's tariffs have already been challenged in the Supreme Court, with some struck down. Critics would argue that aggressive tariffs and transshipment penalties can raise costs for businesses and consumers, and that light assembly in third countries can be legitimate under global trade rules.

The article illustrates a known pattern in modern trade: when tariffs target one country, goods often get rerouted through other countries rather than stopped. That means import data alone may understate China's export reach, while enforcement requires tracing paper trails, factory work, and value added in several countries.

The planned visit by Xi Jinping may lead to new negotiations, but the US also warns that India and other partners could be penalized for transshipment. Future trade frameworks may require stricter origin certification, raising the stakes for smaller economies caught between the US and China.
